---
title: "Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop"
---

We will also use HPC2N or another remote Linux environment. A **remote computer**
is a computer you connect to over the network. Your laptop displays the session;
the remote computer runs the programs and stores the files you save there.

::: {.callout-note}
## Connection details will follow

The teaching team will provide the service, account instructions, login address,
authentication steps, remote-desktop route, and file-transfer instructions.
There is no course login command to run on this page yet.
:::

## Two ways to work remotely

| Connection | What you see | What you use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SSH | A terminal on the remote computer | Navigate folders and run commands. |
| Remote desktop | A graphical workspace on the remote computer | Use a file manager and the applications provided for the course. |

Both give access to a remote environment. Whether they share exactly the same
files depends on how the service is configured; the course instructions will
identify the folders to use.

## What SSH means

SSH is a way to log in securely to another computer. The usual command has
this shape:

```text
ssh your-username@remote-computer-address
```

This is an explanation of the shape, not a working course command. We will
supply the actual address and explain any additional authentication steps.

On Windows you can start SSH from Ubuntu; on Mac use Terminal. Once connected,
commands such as `pwd` and `ls` act on the remote computer. Use `exit` to leave
the SSH session and return to your local shell.

The first connection may ask you to trust the remote computer's host key. Follow
the course's verification instructions before accepting it. Password prompts may
show no characters while you type. Never share passwords or authentication codes.

## Always ask: which computer am I using?

| Question | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Is this terminal local or remote? | It determines where commands run. |
| Which folder am I in? | `pwd` gives the location on that computer. |
| Where did I save the data or report? | Saving remotely does not automatically create a laptop copy. |
| Where is RStudio running? | R needs access to files in its own environment. |

A browser download on your laptop, a file in local Ubuntu, and a file on HPC2N
can be three separate copies. Identical filenames do not make them the same file.
Opening a remote desktop does not automatically transfer your laptop's files.

## What we will practise when access is ready

1. Sign in using the supplied instructions and identify the remote computer.
2. Use `pwd` and `ls`, create a practice folder, and locate a supplied dataset.
3. Leave the SSH session with `exit`, then reconnect and find the folder again.
4. Open the supported remote desktop and find the designated course files.
5. Transfer a small file using the supported route and identify both copies.
6. Open the provided R environment and locate a rendered report.

These are small introductory exercises. Instructions about where programs may
run and how to end the remote-desktop session will accompany the service details.
